title: The SAR Method
author: Blake Harvard
summary: Blake Harvard, who teaches AP Psychology, proposes a simplified three-step model of memory -- Sense, Attend, Rehearse -- as a more accessible entry point than the full technical literature on working memory, cognitive load theory, and Atkinson-Shiffrin's stage model. He walks through each step: sensing information is necessary but not sufficient, since students constantly sense far more stimuli than they can remember; attending is a limited resource that cannot be split across multiple sources, which is why Harvard flatly tells students they cannot effectively multitask while studying; and rehearsing -- through retrieval, discussion, or application -- is what converts attended information into durable memory, since students who appear to understand a lecture often still fail to answer questions on it the next day. Harvard is explicit that SAR is not a comprehensive account of memory, but argues its simplicity is the point: it is content- and age-agnostic, usable as a 30-minute CPD session, a classroom poster, or a quick lesson for any subject or grade. He frames the model as a bridge for teachers and students who want to apply cognitive psychology in the classroom but don't have time to master concepts like element interactivity or the curse of knowledge first.
points: Harvard's Sense-Attend-Rehearse model compresses the technical literature on memory into three steps deliberately simple enough for a classroom poster or a single CPD session.
Attention is a strictly limited resource that cannot be meaningfully split across sources, which is why Harvard tells students bluntly that they cannot effectively multitask while studying.

Rehearsal -- through retrieval, discussion, or application -- is the step that converts attended information into durable memory; without it, students who seemed to understand a lecture often can't answer questions on it the next day.
Harvard positions SAR as content- and age-agnostic, usable identically in a 7th grade science class or a 12th grade language arts class.
quotes: Understanding how we learn via memory processing and understanding what this means for how we study is, in my opinion, of utmost importance to all learners and teachers.
Without a doubt, the first step is sensation. One must sense the information to have any chance of continuing through the memory process.
By choosing to pay attention to the information presented in class, you are giving your brain a chance to understand and encode that information for better understanding.
Do. Not. Multitask. No, you’re not good at it. You’re fibbing to yourself if you believe you are.
The memory of yesterday’s lesson is weak. It needs something to strengthen and increase the likelihood it can be used when required.
This isn't a comprehensive understanding of memory, but I do believe it provides an entry point for students and teachers alike to improve their classroom and/or studying.
